title: Spit-Up vs. Reflux: When It's Just Laundry
hook: Most babies spit up — it's a plumbing issue, not an illness, and a happy, growing 'spitter' needs patience, not treatment. A few specific signs are the ones worth a doctor's call.
key_points: Spit-up (reflux) is very common: the muscle at the top of the stomach is still immature, so milk comes back up easily.
A baby who spits up but feeds well, gains weight, and seems comfortable is a 'happy spitter' — no treatment needed; most outgrow it by 12 months.
Smaller, more frequent feeds, regular burping, and holding baby upright after feeds can reduce how much comes back up.
Call the doctor for poor weight gain, forceful or projectile vomiting, green/bloody vomit, refusing to feed, or back-arching pain — that points beyond simple spit-up.
content_html: Spit-up is one of the most common worries for new parents, and most of the time it's a plumbing issue rather than a sign of illness. The ring of muscle between the stomach and the food pipe is still immature in babies, so when the stomach is full, a little milk slides back up. Doctors call this reflux, and it often peaks around four months and fades as a baby grows.
extra_html: The key question isn't how much a baby spits up but how they're doing. A "happy spitter" — one who feeds well, gains weight, and seems comfortable — needs patience and a cloth, not medicine, and usually grows out of it by the first birthday. You can reduce the volume with smaller, more frequent feeds, burping along the way, and keeping your baby upright for a bit afterward. What does warrant a call to the doctor is a different picture: poor weight gain, forceful or projectile vomiting, vomit that's green, yellow, or bloody, refusing to feed, choking or breathing trouble, or pain and back-arching with feeds. Those suggest reflux disease (GERD) or another cause. This is general guidance — your pediatrician can tell normal spit-up from something that needs treatment.

related.title: Feeding on Demand: Cues and How Often
related.hook: Newborns feed best on demand — watch for early hunger cues rather than the clock, and let wet and dirty diapers, not the exact count of feeds, reassure you they're getting enough.

related.title: Vomiting and Dehydration
related.hook: When a stomach bug hits, the real risk isn't the vomiting itself — it's dehydration. The goal is keeping fluids in with small, frequent sips, and knowing the signs that mean call the doctor.

flashcards.explanation_html: When a baby spits up yet stays comfortable and gains weight, it's a laundry problem, not a medical one. Most outgrow it by their first birthday.

flashcards.prompt: Which sign means spit-up needs a doctor's attention?

choices.text: Forceful/projectile vomiting, poor weight gain, or green or bloody vomit
A small spit-up after most feeds

flashcards.explanation_html: Comfortable spit-up is normal. Projectile or green/bloody vomiting, refusing to feed, pain, or poor weight gain point beyond simple reflux — call the doctor.

flashcards.prompt: What simple measures reduce how much a baby spits up?
flashcards.back_html: Smaller, more frequent feeds, burping during and after feeds, and keeping baby upright for a little while afterward. Don't overfeed.
